title: UNIT 4: REPRODUCTION
notes: Reproduction is the biological process by which organisms produce new individuals of the same species. It ensures continuity of life and transmission of genetic information.

title: 4.1  Introduction to Reproduction
notes:
Reproduction is essential for maintaining populations and passing genetic information to the next generation.

Two main types:
• Asexual reproduction → usually one parent; offspring are genetically very similar to the parent.
• Sexual reproduction → involves formation and fusion of gametes; offspring show genetic variation.

title: 4.2  Asexual Reproduction
notes:
Asexual reproduction produces offspring from a single parent without fusion of gametes.

Characteristics:
• Usually one parent.
• No fertilization.
• Usually rapid.
• Offspring are genetically similar to the parent.
• Useful when conditions are stable.

title: 4.3  Types of Asexual Reproduction
notes:
Major types of asexual reproduction include:
• Fission.
• Fragmentation.
• Budding.
• Vegetative reproduction.
• Parthenogenesis.

The method differs according to the organism and its body structure.

title: 4.3.1  Fission
notes:
Fission is asexual reproduction in which one parent cell or organism divides to form new individuals.

Binary fission → one organism divides into two.
Example → bacteria and Amoeba.

The genetic material is copied before division.

title: 4.3.2  Fragmentation
notes:
Fragmentation occurs when an organism breaks into two or more pieces, and each fragment develops into a complete organism.

Examples:
• Spirogyra.
• Some flatworms.
• Some fungi and algae.

Each fragment must contain the necessary living tissues to regenerate.

title: 4.3.3  Budding
notes:
Budding occurs when a new individual develops as a small outgrowth, or bud, on the parent.

The bud grows and may separate from the parent.

Examples:
• Yeast.
• Hydra.

title: 4.3.4  Vegetative Reproduction
notes:
Vegetative reproduction is asexual reproduction in plants in which new plants develop from vegetative parts such as roots, stems or leaves rather than seeds.

Examples:
• Potato → stem tuber.
• Onion → bulb.
• Strawberry → runner.
• Cassava → stem cutting.

It is widely used in agriculture to produce genetically similar plants.

title: 4.3.5  Parthenogenesis
notes:
Parthenogenesis is the development of an embryo from an unfertilized egg.

It occurs naturally in some animals such as:
• Bees.
• Wasps.
• Aphids.
• Some reptiles.

No fusion of sperm and egg occurs.

title: 4.3.6  Spore Formation (Sporulation)
notes:
Sporulation is asexual reproduction in which an organism produces spores that can develop into new individuals under suitable conditions.

• Spores are usually small, lightweight and resistant to unfavorable conditions.
• Spores are commonly produced by fungi and some plants and microorganisms.
• Example → Rhizopus produces spores in sporangia.

title: 4.3.7  Vegetative Propagation
notes:
Vegetative propagation is asexual reproduction in plants where new plants develop from vegetative organs such as stems, roots or leaves.

Advantages:
• Rapid multiplication.
• Produces plants genetically similar to the parent.
• Useful for propagating plants that do not produce viable seeds.

title: 4.3.7.1  Stolons (Runners)
notes:
Stolons or runners are horizontal stems that grow along or just above the soil surface. New roots and shoots develop at nodes and form new plants.

Example → strawberry.

title: 4.3.7.2  Rhizomes
notes:
A rhizome is a horizontal underground stem that stores food and produces new shoots and roots from its nodes.

Examples → ginger and turmeric.

title: 4.3.7.3  Corms
notes:
A corm is a short, swollen underground stem that stores food. Buds on the corm can develop into new plants.

Examples → gladiolus and taro.

title: 4.3.7.4  Tubers
notes:
A tuber is a swollen underground storage organ, usually a modified stem, containing buds called eyes that can grow into new plants.

Example → potato.

title: 4.3.7.5  Bulbs
notes:
A bulb is a shortened underground stem surrounded by thick, fleshy storage leaves. A bud can develop into a new plant.

Examples → onion and garlic.

title: 4.3.8  Artificial Vegetative Propagation
notes:
Artificial vegetative propagation is the deliberate production of new plants from vegetative parts using human-controlled methods.

Main methods:
• Grafting.
• Cutting.
• Layering.

title: 4.3.8.1  Grafting
notes:
Grafting involves joining a shoot or bud (scion) from one plant to the rooted part (stock) of another compatible plant.

The tissues join and grow as one plant.

Uses:
• Combining desirable characteristics.
• Propagating fruit trees and ornamental plants.

title: 4.3.8.2  Cutting
notes:
Cutting involves placing a piece of a plant, such as a stem, leaf or root, under suitable conditions so that it develops roots and shoots.

Examples → cassava, sugarcane and many ornamental plants.

title: 4.3.8.3  Layering
notes:
Layering involves encouraging roots to develop on a stem while it is still attached to the parent plant. After roots form, the new plant can be separated.

A common method is bending a low branch to the soil and covering part of it with soil.

title: 4.4  Sexual Reproduction in Humans
notes:
Human sexual reproduction involves the production of male and female gametes and their fusion during fertilization.

Male gamete → sperm.
Female gamete → ovum (egg).

Fertilization produces a diploid zygote, which develops through embryonic stages into a new individual.

title: 4.5  Primary and Secondary Sexual Characteristics
notes:
Primary sexual characteristics are reproductive structures and functions directly involved in reproduction and are present or develop during puberty.

Examples:
• Male → testes, penis and sperm production.
• Female → ovaries, uterus and ovulation.

Secondary sexual characteristics develop mainly during puberty and are not directly involved in producing offspring.

Examples:
• Male → deeper voice, facial hair and increased muscle development.
• Female → breast development and widening of the hips.
• Both → increased body hair and other body changes.

title: 4.6  Male Reproductive Structures
notes:
Main structures and functions:
• Testes → produce sperm and testosterone.
• Scrotum → holds testes and helps maintain a suitable temperature for sperm production.
• Epididymis → sperm mature and are stored.
• Vas deferens → transports sperm.
• Seminal vesicles → add nutrient-rich fluid to semen.
• Prostate gland → adds fluid that supports sperm function.
• Bulbourethral glands → secrete lubricating fluid.
• Urethra → passage for semen and urine at different times.
• Penis → transfers semen into the female reproductive tract.

title: 4.7  Female Reproductive Structures
notes:
Main structures and functions:
• Ovaries → produce ova and hormones such as estrogen and progesterone.
• Fallopian tubes → transport the ovum; fertilization usually occurs here.
• Uterus → site of implantation and development of the embryo and fetus.
• Endometrium → inner uterine lining that changes during the menstrual cycle.
• Cervix → lower opening of the uterus.
• Vagina → receives penis/semen and serves as the birth canal.

title: 4.8  The Menstrual Cycle
notes:
The menstrual cycle is a repeating series of changes in the ovaries and uterus, commonly about 28 days but varying among individuals.

Main stages:
1. Menstruation → shedding of the uterine lining.
2. Follicular phase → ovarian follicles develop; estrogen rises.
3. Ovulation → release of a mature ovum, triggered by an LH surge.
4. Luteal phase → corpus luteum produces progesterone, helping maintain the uterine lining.

If fertilization does not occur, hormone levels fall and menstruation begins.

title: 4.9  Fertilization and Pregnancy
notes:
Fertilization is the fusion of a sperm and an egg, usually occurring in the fallopian tube.

Sperm + ovum → zygote.

The zygote undergoes cell division and develops into an embryo. It implants in the uterine lining, where pregnancy continues as the embryo develops into a fetus.

The placenta allows exchange of oxygen, nutrients and wastes between maternal and fetal blood without normally mixing the two blood supplies directly.

title: 4.10  Methods of Birth Control
notes:
Birth control methods prevent pregnancy by preventing ovulation, blocking sperm, preventing fertilization or preventing implantation.

Methods include:
• Condoms → barrier method; also reduce the risk of many STIs.
• Oral contraceptive pills → mainly prevent ovulation.
• Injectable contraceptives → provide hormones for pregnancy prevention.
• Implants → release hormones over an extended period.
• Intrauterine devices (IUDs) → placed in the uterus to prevent pregnancy.
• Emergency contraception → reduces pregnancy risk after unprotected sex when used promptly.
• Sterilization → permanent contraception.

Effectiveness and suitability vary by method.

title: 4.10.1  Diaphragm
notes:
A diaphragm is a flexible barrier placed inside the vagina to cover the cervix and prevent sperm from entering the uterus.

• It is a barrier contraceptive.
• It is commonly used with spermicide.
• It does not protect reliably against STIs.

title: 4.10.2  Spermicides
notes:
Spermicides are chemical contraceptives that immobilize or destroy sperm.

• Available as creams, gels, foams, films or suppositories.
• Often used with barrier methods.
• Used alone, they are generally less effective than many other contraceptive methods.
• Do not protect against STIs.

title: 4.10.3  Contraceptive Pill
notes:
The contraceptive pill contains hormones that mainly prevent ovulation and also make fertilization less likely.

• Taken regularly according to the prescribed schedule.
• Does not protect against STIs.
• Effectiveness depends on correct and consistent use.

title: 4.10.4  Surgical Methods of Birth Control
notes: Surgical contraception involves permanently blocking or cutting reproductive pathways to prevent fertilization.

title: 4.10.5  Male Sterilization — Vasectomy
notes:
Vasectomy is a permanent contraceptive procedure in which the vas deferens are cut, blocked or sealed.

• Prevents sperm from entering the semen.
• Testosterone production and sexual function are generally not stopped.
• It does not protect against STIs.
• It is not immediately effective; alternative contraception is needed until follow-up confirms success.

title: 4.10.6  Female Sterilization — Laparotomy
notes:
Female sterilization blocks or cuts the fallopian tubes so sperm cannot normally reach the egg.

Laparotomy is a surgical approach involving an abdominal incision that can be used to access the reproductive organs.

• Prevents fertilization.
• Does not normally stop ovarian hormone production or menstruation.
• Intended as permanent contraception.
• Does not protect against STIs.

title: 4.11  Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
notes:
Sexually transmitted infections are infections that can spread mainly through sexual contact.

Examples:
• HIV infection.
• Syphilis.
• Gonorrhea.
• Chlamydia.
• Genital herpes.
• Human papillomavirus (HPV).
• Trichomoniasis.

Some STIs may have no symptoms, so testing is important when exposure is possible.

title: 4.11.2  Trichomoniasis
notes:
Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the parasite Trichomonas vaginalis.

Transmission → mainly through sexual contact.

Possible symptoms:
• Genital irritation or itching.
• Unusual discharge.
• Pain during urination or sex.
• Many infected people may have no symptoms.

Prevention → safer sex practices, testing and treatment of infected partners.

title: 4.11.3  Chlamydia
notes:
Chlamydia is a bacterial STI caused by Chlamydia trachomatis.

• Often causes no symptoms.
• Can cause abnormal genital discharge or painful urination.
• Untreated infection can lead to serious reproductive complications.

Prevention → condoms, testing, limiting exposure and prompt treatment of infected people and partners.

title: 4.11.4  Gonorrhea
notes:
Gonorrhea is a bacterial STI caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Possible symptoms:
• Painful urination.
• Genital discharge.
• Pelvic or testicular pain.
• Some infections have no symptoms.

Prevention → condoms, appropriate testing and prompt treatment. Antibiotic resistance makes proper medical treatment important.

title: 4.11.5  Syphilis
notes:
Syphilis is a bacterial STI caused by Treponema pallidum.

It can progress through stages:
• Primary → often a painless sore.
• Secondary → possible rash and other symptoms.
• Latent → symptoms may disappear while infection remains.
• Untreated late infection → may damage organs and the nervous system.

It can also pass from a pregnant person to the fetus.

Prevention → safer sex, testing and prompt medical treatment.

title: 4.11.1  STI Transmission and Prevention
notes:
STIs can spread through vaginal, anal or oral sexual contact and, depending on the infection, through blood or from mother to child during pregnancy or childbirth.

Prevention:
• Abstinence eliminates sexual transmission.
• Mutual long-term monogamy with an uninfected partner reduces risk.
• Correct and consistent condom use reduces the risk of many STIs.
• Get tested when appropriate.
• Avoid sharing needles or other equipment that may contain blood.
• Get available vaccines such as HPV and hepatitis B vaccines.
• Seek medical testing and treatment when symptoms or exposure occur.

title: UNIT 4 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
Asexual reproduction → one parent, no gamete fusion, usually little genetic variation.

Fission → division into new individuals.
Fragmentation → pieces develop into new organisms.
Budding → new organism grows from a bud.
Vegetative reproduction → new plants from roots, stems or leaves.
Parthenogenesis → embryo develops from an unfertilized egg.

Sexual reproduction → fusion of male and female gametes.
Sperm + ovum → zygote.

Male:
Testes → sperm + testosterone.
Epididymis → sperm maturation/storage.
Vas deferens → sperm transport.

Female:
Ovaries → ova + hormones.
Fallopian tube → usual site of fertilization.
Uterus → implantation and fetal development.

Menstrual cycle:
Menstruation → follicular phase → ovulation → luteal phase.

 EXAM TIP:
Fertilization usually occurs in the fallopian tube, while implantation occurs in the uterus.
